7020:
Glowering means having a look — or giving off a feeling — that is deeply angry, dark, and threatening, usually in a silent, brooding way.

When something or someone is described as glowering, they are not just mildly upset or frowning. They carry a heavy, intense, almost burning sense of anger or menace — the kind that doesn't need to shout to feel dangerous.

Picture this: someone has just heard something that made them furious. They don't scream. They don't cry. They go very still. Their brows pull together and drop low over their eyes. Their jaw tightens. Their eyes become hard, dark, and fixed — like two points of concentrated heat locked onto a target. That expression — that silent, smouldering, hostile stare — is a glowering look.

It is the face of a person who is so angry that the anger has turned inward, become dense and controlled, and is now radiating outward like heat from a fire. The mouth is not shouting. The eyes are doing all the work.

Glowering always contains two things working together:

1. Anger or hostility — This is not sadness, not confusion, not boredom. It is specifically a dark, negative, threatening emotion.

2. Intensity — It is not a light frown. It is heavy. Concentrated. The kind that fills a room and makes people uncomfortable just by being there.

Take either ingredient away, and the word no longer fits. A mild frown is not glowering. Loud, explosive rage is not glowering either — that's too wild and loose. Glowering sits in between: controlled, dark, and quietly terrifying.
It Can Describe More Than Just Faces

While glowering most commonly describes a person's expression or look, it can also describe:

A person's overall presence or posture:

"A glowering figure stood in the doorway."

Here, the whole person — not just their face — gives off a dark, menacing energy. You can sense the anger in the way they stand, the way they occupy space.

The sky or weather:

"Glowering clouds gathered on the horizon."
"The hikers looked up at the glowering sky."

When used this way, it means the sky looks dark, heavy, and threatening — like a storm is coming. It borrows the human feeling of menace and applies it to nature. A glowering sky doesn't just look grey; it looks angry, like it's about to unleash something.

This is what makes the word elegant: it transfers the feeling of a person's hostile stare onto the natural world, and it works perfectly.

One of the most important things about glowering is what it is not doing: it is not speaking.

A glowering look is almost always silent. It is the anger of someone who has not yet acted, has not yet erupted. This gives the word a quality of threat and suspense. You feel the danger, but it hasn't been released yet. This is what separates glowering from words like raging or furious — those words suggest the emotion has burst open. Glowering is the emotion held tightly, aimed like a weapon.
How It Compares to Similar Words

• Frowning — simply having a downward expression; could be confusion, sadness, or mild disapproval. Much weaker than glowering.
  • Scowling — the closest cousin; an angry, wrinkled frown. Scowling and glowering overlap significantly, but glowering has a slightly darker, more brooding, and more threatening quality to it. Scowling is the expression; glowering is the expression plus the intense emotional weight behind it.
  • Menacing — threatening in a general sense. Glowering is a specific kind of menace expressed through a look.
  • Brooding — thinking deeply in a gloomy, dark way. A person can be brooding without being angry. But glowering always involves anger or hostility.

"He gave her a glowering look when she interrupted him for the third time."

— His stare was dark, angry, and deeply unfriendly.

"The glowering man in the corner made the other guests nervous."

— He wasn't doing anything, but his expression and presence radiated hostility.

"She sat in silence, her glowering expression warning everyone to stay away."

— No words needed; the look said everything.

"The children abandoned their plans for a picnic when they saw the glowering sky."

— The dark, threatening clouds made it clear a storm was near.
The Feeling It Creates in a Reader

When a writer uses the word glowering, they are doing something very specific: they are making you feel a quiet dread. Not the sharp, sudden dread of a shout or a crash — but the slow, creeping dread of knowing something dangerous is right there, watching, waiting. It is one of those rare words that not only describes a feeling but actually produces a version of that feeling in the reader.

If you had to summarise it in the simplest terms possible:

Glowering = a dark, silent, intensely angry look (or presence) that feels threatening just by existing.

That's the heart of it. Everything else — the brooding quality, the silence, the weather usage — flows naturally from that core.
7021: The word glowing comes from the idea of something that produces a warm, soft, steady light — like hot coals in a fire, or a lamp in a dark room. That image of warmth, brightness, and richness is the heart of this word. Whether you use it literally or figuratively, that same feeling of something being full, warm, and radiantly positive runs through every single meaning.
Meaning 1: Producing or Reflecting Warm, Steady Light

The most direct meaning of glowing is describing something that emits or reflects a warm, soft light — not a harsh, blinding light, but a gentle, rich, steady one.

Examples:

  • The glowing embers of the campfire kept us warm through the night.
  • She stared at the glowing screen of her phone in the dark bedroom.
  • The city looked beautiful, with glowing streetlights reflecting on the wet road.

Key feeling here: It's not explosive or flickering. It's steady, warm, and continuous. A lightning bolt is not glowing. A candle flame is.
Meaning 2: Very Warm and Attractive in Color

When describing colors, glowing means colors that are vivid, rich, deep, and warm — colors that seem to have light coming from within them, almost like they're alive.

Examples:

  • The autumn leaves turned glowing shades of red, orange, and gold.
  • The painting was full of glowing colours — warm pinks and deep purples.
  • The sunset lit the sky in glowing tones that made everyone stop and stare.

Key feeling here: These are not pale or dull colors. They are saturated, rich, and radiant. Think of the difference between a faded old photograph and a vivid, fresh painting — the latter has glowing colors.
Meaning 3: Looking Radiant Due to Health or Happiness (describing a person)

When glowing describes a person's appearance, it means they look visibly healthy, happy, warm, or full of life — their face has a warmth and brightness to it that comes from inside.

Examples:

  • She came back from her holiday looking absolutely glowing.
  • He was glowing with pride after his son won the award.
  • The bride looked glowing on her wedding day.
  • After months of eating well and exercising, she had a glowing complexion.

Key feeling here: It suggests a kind of inner light. The person doesn't just look fine — they look genuinely radiant, as if happiness or health is literally shining through their skin. This is why people often say a pregnant woman is "glowing" — she appears unusually bright and full of life.

You'll often see these phrases:

  • glowing with pride
  • glowing with health
  • glowing with excitement
  • glowing complexion (skin that looks healthy and radiant)
Meaning 4: Extremely Enthusiastic and Positive (describing praise, reviews, or reports)

This is perhaps the most widely used meaning of glowing in everyday language. When praise, a review, a report, or a description is called glowing, it means it is extremely positive, full of admiration, and warm in its approval — not just "good," but enthusiastically, generously complimentary.

Examples:

  • The restaurant received glowing reviews from every food critic in the city.
  • Her professor wrote a glowing letter of recommendation for her university application.
  • The new film got glowing praise from audiences worldwide.
  • His performance was described in glowing terms by all his colleagues.
  • The report on the company's progress was absolutely glowing.

Key feeling here: When something gets a glowing review or description, it means whoever is giving the feedback is not holding back — they are genuinely and fully impressed. It goes beyond "positive" — it means warmly enthusiastic and full of admiration.

Notice the phrase: "in glowing terms" — this is a very common expression meaning "in an extremely positive and admiring way."

  • She spoke about her mentor in glowing terms.

This is important for a learner to understand: "glowing" is always positive. There is no negative or neutral glowing. It carries a sense of warmth, richness, and genuine appreciation in every context. If someone says something is glowing, you should immediately know it's being presented in the best possible light.

Compare these:

  • A good review → positive, but ordinary
  • A positive review → clearly favourable
  • A glowing review → enthusiastic, warm, and generously admiring

The word glowing always feels like an upgrade. It suggests not just approval, but genuine, warm, full-hearted admiration.

• Bright simply means having a lot of light or being vivid. Glowing adds warmth and steadiness to that.
  • Shining suggests reflected or emitted light but can be sharp and cold (like metal). Glowing is always warm.
  • Radiant is very close to glowing in both the physical and figurative senses, but radiant often suggests something more outwardly expressive, whereas glowing can feel slightly more internal and steady.
  • Flattering (for praise) just means something makes you look good. Glowing means it does so with great warmth and enthusiasm.

The single thread connecting all four meanings of glowing is this idea of something being warm, full, rich, and radiantly positive — whether that's a fire, a color, a person's face, or someone's praise. Once you hold that image in your mind, the word will feel natural in any context you encounter it.
7022: Glum means quietly sad, downcast, or unhappy — in a way that shows on your face and in your body. A glum person is not screaming or crying dramatically. Instead, they are silent, withdrawn, and visibly low in spirit. Think of someone sitting with their shoulders drooped, their face expressionless or slightly frowning, not saying much, and clearly not in a good mood. That is the picture of someone who is glum.
What It Actually Feels Like (or Looks Like)

Glum is a specific type of sadness. It has two sides to it:

On the inside: A glum person feels deflated, low, and cheerless. Not necessarily devastated or broken — just flat, heavy, and joyless. The energy is drained out of them.

On the outside: It shows. A glum person often has a dull, downcast expression. They go quiet. They don't smile. They might stare blankly or look at the floor. Their mood is written all over their face and posture.

This is important: glum is almost always visible. You can see someone being glum. It's not a hidden inner feeling — it surfaces outward.
How Glum Differs from Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

Glum vs. Sad:
"Sad" is a broad, general word for any kind of unhappiness. Glum is more specific — it points to a quiet, withdrawn, sullen kind of sadness. All glum people are sad, but not all sad people are glum. Someone crying at a funeral is sad, but not necessarily glum. Someone sitting quietly in a corner after bad news, saying nothing, looking blank — that is glum.

Glum vs. Sullen:
Both words describe a quiet, withdrawn bad mood. But "sullen" carries a stronger sense of resentment or silent anger. A sullen person might be refusing to talk because they are annoyed at someone. A glum person is simply down and dejected — there's no real anger in it, just low spirits.

Glum vs. Depressed:
"Depressed" is far more serious and intense. Clinical depression is a deep, long-lasting condition. Glum is typically a lighter, temporary state — a bad mood, a low moment, a short episode of feeling down. You can be glum for an afternoon. Depression can last months or years.

Glum vs. Melancholy:
"Melancholy" is deeper, more emotional, and sometimes even carries a poetic or beautiful quality to it — like a soft, lingering sadness. Glum is plainer and more everyday. It is simply low and droopy, nothing poetic about it.

Think of sadness on a scale:

Disappointed → Glum → Sad → Dejected → Despondent → Devastated

Glum sits in the lower-to-middle range. It is more than just slight disappointment, but it is nowhere near heartbreak or despair. It is that "blah," heavy, low-energy feeling that makes you go quiet and look downcast.
What Can Be Described as Glum?

A person: The most common use.

"He was glum all evening after losing the match."

A face or expression:

"She had a glum look on her face when she saw the results."

A mood or silence:

"There was a glum silence in the room after the announcement."

An atmosphere or place (less common, but valid — meaning cheerless and dull):

"The waiting room felt glum and lifeless."

• "Why are you so glum today? Did something happen?" — Asking someone why they look low and withdrawn.
  • "The children were glum when they heard the trip was cancelled." — They went quiet and downcast.
  • "She sat alone at the table, glum and lost in her own thoughts." — Withdrawn, visibly low in spirit.
  • "Even good news didn't seem to lift his glum mood." — His flat, joyless state wouldn't shift.
  • "Don't look so glum — things will get better!" — An encouragement to cheer up from a visibly sad expression.

Glum = quietly sad and visibly down in spirit, in a subdued, withdrawn way — not dramatic, not violent, just flat, heavy, and low.

If you remember that image — a person sitting quietly, face drooping, saying little, the spark gone from their eyes — you will never misuse or misunderstand this word.
7023:
A glut means an extremely large supply of something — so much of it that it far exceeds what people actually need or want. Think of it simply as: too much of something, more than can reasonably be used or absorbed.

The key idea is excess that causes a problem. A glut isn't just "having plenty" — it's having so much that it creates a burden, waste, or a collapse in value.

Imagine a small town with 10 pizza shops but only enough residents to keep 3 of them busy. That's a glut of pizza shops. Or picture a farm that produces 10,000 apples, but the local market can only sell 2,000. The remaining 8,000 sit unsold and rot — that's a glut of apples.

The word is most commonly used in economics and markets, but it works across many everyday situations too.
What Happens When There's a Glut?

A glut typically sets off a chain of consequences. Because supply is far greater than demand, sellers must compete harder with each other. This competition drives prices down, sometimes so low that producers stop making any profit. Some goods may go unsold, stockpiled, or wasted.

For example: if oil-producing countries pump far more oil than the world actually consumes, there is a glut of oil on the market. Prices crash, and oil companies earn far less money. This is exactly what happened in the 1980s and again in 2020.
How It's Used in a Sentence

The word "glut" almost always follows the pattern "a glut of [something]" or "a glut on the market." Here are real-world style examples:

  • "The record harvest led to a glut of wheat, and farmers were forced to sell at a loss." — Great production, but far more than the market could absorb.
  • "There is a glut of streaming services today — more than viewers can realistically subscribe to." — More services exist than the market actually needs.
  • "After universities churned out too many law graduates, a glut of lawyers found themselves unable to find work in their field." — Supply of lawyers far exceeded demand.
  • "A glut of unsold homes in the city pushed property prices down sharply." — Too many houses, too few buyers.
  • "The tech boom created a glut of office space, leaving buildings half-empty."

"Glut" carries a distinctly negative, problem-signaling tone. When someone says there is a glut of something, they almost always mean it is causing trouble — falling prices, wasted resources, a saturated market, or widespread unemployment in a profession.

Notice the difference in feeling between these two sentences:

  • "There is an abundance of fresh fruit at the market." → Positive. Plenty of good things.
  • "There is a glut of fresh fruit at the market." → Negative. So much fruit that sellers can't offload it, prices have collapsed, and much of it will go to waste.

Same situation, completely different emotional weight.
How Glut Differs from Similar Words

Surplus is the closest word. A surplus simply means "more than needed," but it can be neutral or even positive — a country can hold a grain surplus that it exports profitably. A glut is more extreme: the excess is so large and unmanageable that it is actively causing problems.

Abundance is a positive word — lots of good things, and everyone benefits. A glut is not positive.

Oversupply is nearly identical to glut in meaning and the two are often interchangeable. However, "glut" is more vivid and emotive — it conveys the sense of being overwhelmed or flooded.

Shortage is the direct opposite of a glut — not enough of something, rather than too much.

A glut = an overwhelming excess of something that causes real problems, most often seen as crashing prices, waste, or a market that is completely flooded. It almost always appears as "a glut of X" and always signals that this surplus is a bad thing, not a happy one.
7024:
To glut something means to fill it far beyond what it needs or can handle — to flood it with an overwhelming excess until it is completely stuffed, saturated, or overwhelmed.

The key word here is excess. Glut is not about simply filling something. It is about overfilling it to the point where what has been added becomes a burden, a problem, or causes things to slow down, break down, or lose value.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. To glut a market (or a place / a system)

This is the most common use. When you glut a market, you flood it with so much supply of something that the market cannot absorb it all. There is simply more of the thing available than people want or need. As a result, the excess sits unused, prices drop, and the whole system feels overwhelmed.

Examples:

  • Cheap imports glutted the domestic steel market, causing prices to collapse.
  • A record harvest glutted the grain market, leaving farmers unable to sell at a profit.
  • Streaming platforms have glutted the entertainment industry with content, making it hard for any single show to stand out.

In each case, the supply has been pushed so far beyond demand that the market is now drowning in it.

2. To glut oneself (or to glut an appetite / a desire)

Here, glut means to satisfy a craving, appetite, or desire so completely — and so excessively — that you tip over into a state of being overfull, weary, or even disgusted. You don't just satisfy yourself; you indulge yourself beyond the point of satisfaction.

Examples:

  • He glutted himself on rich food during the festival and felt ill for days afterward.
  • She glutted her curiosity by reading every book on the subject she could find.
  • The soldiers had glutted their desire for revenge and now felt only emptiness.

Notice that in all three examples, the satisfaction has gone too far. There is always a sense that the indulgence crossed a line — it became too much.

Glut almost always carries a negative or at least cautionary tone. It suggests that a limit has been crossed. Think of it as the difference between quenching your thirst and drinking until you feel sick. Glut lives on the "sick" side of that line.

When a market is glutted, it is not thriving — it is struggling under too much supply.
When a person gluttes themselves, they are not pleasantly full — they are overwhelmed, weary, or regretful.

You will very frequently encounter glut in the passive voice: "glutted with." This is one of the most natural ways the word appears.

  • The market is glutted with used cars.
  • The city was glutted with tourists.
  • Her mind was glutted with information after the all-day seminar.

"Glutted with" simply means: overwhelmed by an excess of something.
The Subtle but Important Distinction from Similar Words

• Fill → neutral. Just means to put things in until there is no more space.
  • Flood → emphasises the sudden, overwhelming rush of something.
  • Saturate → means to fill something so completely that nothing more can be absorbed.
  • Glut → specifically emphasises that the excess has become a problem — prices fall, pleasure turns to discomfort, or the system cannot function properly. It is excess that hurts.

To glut is to supply, fill, or indulge something so far beyond its capacity or need that the excess itself becomes the problem — whether that is a market drowning in oversupply or a person made sick by overindulgence.
7025: When you describe something as gluten-free, you are saying that it does not contain gluten, or that it contains only a trace amount of gluten so tiny it is considered safe to ignore. The word "free" here works exactly like it does in words like "sugar-free" or "fat-free" — it means without, or absent of. So gluten-free = without gluten.

To truly understand "gluten-free," you first need to understand gluten itself.

Gluten is a natural protein — a substance found in certain grains. The main grains that contain it are:

  • Wheat (the most common source — used in bread, pasta, cakes, cookies, biscuits, chapati, naan, and most flour-based foods)
  • Barley (used in beer, malt, and some soups)
  • Rye (used in some breads and cereals)

When wheat flour is mixed with water and kneaded, gluten is what gives dough its stretchy, chewy, elastic quality. It's what holds bread together and gives it that soft, spongy texture. Without gluten, bread would crumble and fall apart.

Oats are a special case — oats themselves do not naturally contain gluten, but they are often grown on the same fields as wheat or processed in the same factories, so they frequently get contaminated with wheat. This is why oats are sometimes avoided too, unless specifically labeled "gluten-free oats."
Who Needs Gluten-Free Things, and Why?

This is where the adjective becomes especially important in everyday life. Not everyone needs to avoid gluten — but for some people, it is medically essential, and for others, it is a lifestyle choice.

1. People with Celiac Disease (a serious medical condition)

Celiac disease is an autoimmune condition. When a person with celiac disease eats even a tiny amount of gluten, their immune system treats it as an enemy and attacks the lining of their small intestine. Over time, this causes serious damage — the intestine can no longer absorb nutrients properly, leading to malnutrition, chronic pain, fatigue, and many other problems. There is no medicine or cure for celiac disease. The only treatment is to completely avoid gluten for life. For these people, "gluten-free" is not a preference — it is a medical necessity.

2. People with Non-Celiac Gluten Sensitivity

Some people do not have celiac disease, but they still feel unwell after eating gluten — they may experience bloating, stomach pain, headaches, or tiredness. This is called non-celiac gluten sensitivity. Their intestines are not being permanently damaged the way they are in celiac disease, but they genuinely feel better when they avoid gluten. The adjective "gluten-free" helps them identify safe foods.

3. People with a Wheat Allergy

This is different from celiac disease. A wheat allergy is an immune reaction to proteins in wheat (not necessarily gluten specifically). These people must also avoid wheat-containing foods, so "gluten-free" labels are helpful — though they need to be careful, because gluten-free does not always mean wheat-free (barley and rye also contain gluten but are not wheat).

4. People Who Choose to Avoid Gluten

Some people avoid gluten simply because they believe it makes them feel healthier or lighter, even if they have no diagnosed medical condition. This is a personal lifestyle choice. For them, "gluten-free" is more of a dietary preference than a necessity.

The adjective "gluten-free" almost always comes before a noun, or after a linking verb like "is" or "are."

  • "This is a gluten-free cake." (before the noun "cake")
  • "The pasta is gluten-free." (after the linking verb "is")
  • "She follows a gluten-free diet."
  • "We only stock gluten-free products."
  • "Is this bread gluten-free?"

Many whole, unprocessed foods are naturally gluten-free — they simply never contained gluten to begin with:

  • Grains and starches: Rice, corn (maize), potatoes, quinoa, millet, sorghum, tapioca, buckwheat
  • Proteins: All plain meats, poultry, fish, eggs, legumes (lentils, chickpeas, beans)
  • Dairy: Plain milk, cheese, butter, plain yogurt
  • Produce: All fresh fruits and vegetables
  • Fats and oils: All plain oils, butter

Foods that commonly contain gluten include most breads, rotis made from wheat flour, pasta, noodles, pizza, cakes, cookies, crackers, most breakfast cereals, beer, soy sauce, and many gravies and soups (because wheat flour is often used to thicken them).

In many countries, "gluten-free" is not just an informal word — it is a regulated label. Governments have set strict rules about when a product can legally carry this label on its packaging.

In most places (including the United States, European Union, and India), a food can officially be labeled "gluten-free" only if it contains less than 20 parts per million (ppm) of gluten.

To understand 20 ppm: imagine one million tiny pieces of food — if fewer than 20 of those pieces are gluten, the food qualifies. This is an extraordinarily small amount. It was chosen because scientific research has shown that most people with celiac disease can tolerate this level without harm. A product that intentionally contains gluten — even a small amount — cannot legally use this label.

This regulatory definition is why the word carries real weight and is not just casual advertising language.

Even a food that has no gluten as an ingredient can sometimes become contaminated with gluten. This is called cross-contamination. For example, if gluten-free bread is baked in the same oven or cut with the same knife as regular wheat bread, tiny particles of gluten can transfer onto the gluten-free bread. For people with celiac disease, even this tiny contamination can cause harm.

This is why you will sometimes see food labels say "certified gluten-free" or "made in a gluten-free facility" — these phrases tell you that extra care was taken to prevent cross-contamination, not just that the recipe itself avoids gluten ingredients.

Gluten-free means: containing no gluten, or containing gluten at a level so low (under 20 ppm) it is officially considered safe for people who must avoid it.

It describes food, drinks, diets, menus, kitchens, and lifestyles. It is used by people who must avoid gluten for medical reasons (celiac disease, gluten sensitivity, wheat allergy) and by those who choose to avoid it for personal health preferences. It is a legally regulated term in most countries, meaning companies cannot put it on a label carelessly — the product must genuinely meet the standard.
7026:
Glutinous means sticky, thick, and glue-like in texture — the kind of stickiness where something clings to your fingers, stretches when you pull it, and resists coming off cleanly. Think of honey dripping slowly from a spoon, or the way cooked oatmeal sticks to a bowl. That quality — that thick, clinging, adhesive consistency — is what "glutinous" captures.

If something is glutinous, it behaves a lot like glue: it sticks, it's gooey, it pulls and clings.
What It Feels and Looks Like

To really feel the word, picture these sensations:

  • You touch something and it grabs your finger slightly.
  • When you pull your finger away, the substance either stretches or leaves a sticky trace.
  • It's not just wet — it's clingingly wet, with a thickness and body to it.
  • It pours slowly, not freely.

That combination of thickness + stickiness + clinginess is the heart of "glutinous."

1. Food — most commonly
This is by far the most frequent use. Foods can be glutinous when cooked or processed in a way that makes them sticky and dense.

  • Glutinous rice (also called sticky rice) is a famous example — when cooked, the grains stick together in a clumpy, gluey mass rather than staying separate and fluffy like regular rice. It's widely used in Asian cuisines.
  • Overcooked pasta can become glutinous — thick, gummy, and sticking to itself.
  • Certain puddings, porridges, and dumplings are described as glutinous because of their dense, sticky texture.
  • Melted marshmallows, caramel sauce, or thick syrup are all glutinous.

2. Natural substances

  • Wet clay and mud after heavy rain can be glutinous — heavy, sticky, sucking at your boots.
  • Tree sap or resin is often glutinous — thick, slow, and clingy.
  • Some insects produce glutinous secretions to trap prey.

3. Any sticky, viscous material in general
A scientist might describe a lab substance as glutinous. A chef might warn that a sauce has become glutinous. A writer might describe a swamp as having glutinous mud. The word fits anywhere the idea of thick, clinging stickiness applies.

Glutinous sits in the moderate-to-high range of stickiness. It's not the light, surface-level tackiness of a Post-it note. It's a heavier, more enveloping stickiness — the kind that slows things down and makes them cling together. But it's not necessarily as rigid or bonding as actual glue. Think of it as behaving like glue rather than being glue.

These words overlap with glutinous but each has a slightly different shade:

  • Sticky — the broadest, most everyday word. Glutinous is a more specific and formal version of sticky, emphasizing thickness and a glue-like quality.
  • Viscous — refers mainly to how slowly a liquid flows (like thick syrup or oil). Glutinous adds the element of stickiness on top of that thickness.
  • Gluey — almost a synonym, informal. Glutinous is the more refined word.
  • Gooey — informal, often used affectionately (gooey chocolate cake). Glutinous is more neutral or clinical.
  • Gelatinous — jelly-like and wobbly (like Jell-O). Gelatinous things jiggle; glutinous things stick. They can overlap, but they're not the same.
  • Mucilaginous — sticky and slimy like mucus (okra is a good example). More biological/organic in feel.
A Very Common Mistake to Avoid

Because the word looks similar to "gluten", many people assume that glutinous means containing gluten (the protein found in wheat). This is incorrect.

Glutinous refers purely to a texture — the sticky, gluey quality. It says nothing about the presence or absence of the protein gluten. In fact, glutinous rice is typically considered gluten-free, even though its very name has "glut-" in it. The name comes from its glue-like, sticky texture — not from gluten the protein. This is one of the most important things to know about this word.

• "The porridge had been left on the stove too long and had turned glutinous and thick."
  • "She pulled her boot out of the glutinous mud with a loud sucking sound."
  • "The dumplings were made with glutinous rice flour, giving them their famously chewy, sticky skin."
  • "The syrup reduced until it became a glutinous, dark caramel that coated the back of the spoon."
  • "The wound was sealed with a glutinous substance secreted by the insect."
Glutinous means having the thick, sticky, clinging quality of glue — used to describe foods, substances, or materials that stick together, adhere to surfaces, and resist flowing or separating freely.
7027:
A glutton is a person who eats or drinks far more than what is normal or necessary — not simply someone with a big appetite, but someone who consumes in an excessive, greedy, and unrestrained way. The key idea is not just quantity but lack of control. Most people feel full and naturally stop eating. A glutton ignores that signal and keeps going, driven by greed or craving rather than genuine hunger.

Example: He had already finished two large meals and still went back for more. Everyone at the table was staring at the glutton.

Calling someone a glutton is not neutral — it is a criticism. It implies that the person lacks self-discipline and self-control. You are not merely describing how much they eat; you are commenting on their character. Historically, gluttony (the act or habit of a glutton) has been regarded as a moral failing, one of the famous "seven deadly sins." Because of this history, the word carries a weight of moral disapproval that a phrase like "big eater" simply does not.
When it is used figuratively (beyond food)

Over time, "glutton" expanded well beyond food. Today it is regularly used to describe anyone who consumes, seeks, or pursues anything in excessive amounts. The food is gone; the idea of insatiable greed remains.

Example: She reads six books a week and still wants more. She is a glutton for literature.

Example: He watches ten hours of television a day. A true glutton for entertainment.

The logic is always the same: too much, too greedily, without restraint.
The most common expression: "a glutton for punishment"

This is the phrase you will encounter most often in everyday English. A glutton for punishment is someone who willingly takes on pain, difficulty, suffering, or hardship — almost as if they enjoy it, seek it out, or simply cannot stop themselves from putting their hand back in the fire.

Example: She ran her fourth marathon this year despite injuring her knee in the last one. She is a glutton for punishment.

This phrase can be used critically (to suggest someone is reckless or stubborn) but is very often used with humor or even admiration — a playful way of saying someone is unusually tough, driven, or relentless. Similarly, you will hear "a glutton for work" (someone who works obsessively), "a glutton for attention" (someone who constantly craves the spotlight), and "a glutton for praise" (someone who endlessly seeks compliments). In all these cases, the structure is the same: a glutton for something means a person who can never get enough of that thing.

The tone of "glutton" shifts depending on context. Used seriously, it is a sharp criticism of greed and weakness of character. Used in a lighthearted or joking way — between friends at a dinner table, for instance — it softens considerably and is closer to teasing. Context will almost always make the intention clear.
The related word forms you need to know

Gluttony is the noun that describes the habit, act, or quality itself rather than the person. "The banquet descended into pure gluttony." Gluttonous is the adjective form, used to describe a person or behavior characterized by this kind of excess. "His gluttonous appetite alarmed his doctor." Gluttonously is the adverb. "She ate gluttonously, barely pausing between bites."

"Glutton" is also the common name for the wolverine, a powerfully built wild mammal known for its ferocious and voracious feeding behavior. The animal was named after the word, not the other way around — people observed how aggressively it ate and called it a glutton. If you ever encounter the word used in the context of wildlife or nature, this is what it refers to.
7028:
Before you can understand the idiom, you need to understand the word glutton.

A glutton is a person who eats a huge, excessive amount of food — far more than any normal person would. They don't just eat when they're hungry. They keep eating and eating, almost as if they enjoy the discomfort of being stuffed. They can't get enough.

So the word "glutton" carries a core idea: someone who craves and keeps consuming something to an extreme degree.
Now, What Does the Idiom Mean?

When you call someone "a glutton for punishment," you are saying that this person willingly and repeatedly takes on pain, hardship, difficulty, or unpleasant situations — almost as if they enjoy it, or at least don't mind it at all.

Just like a food glutton can't stop eating, a glutton for punishment can't stop seeking out hard, exhausting, or painful experiences — even when nobody is forcing them to.

In short: they keep asking for more difficulty than any reasonable person would want.
The Core Logic of the Idiom

Think of it this way:

  • A glutton eats too much food → they invite physical discomfort on themselves.
  • A glutton for punishment takes on too much hardship → they invite suffering or difficulty on themselves.

The word "punishment" here doesn't mean literal punishment from a teacher or a court. It means anything that is tough, painful, exhausting, or unpleasant — hard work, emotional stress, physical strain, difficult situations, etc.
The Tone: Is It an Insult?

This is important. The idiom is almost never a harsh insult. Its tone is almost always one of the following:

1. Affectionate teasing — You say it about someone you respect, with a smile. You admire their toughness but find it a little crazy.

"You ran your third marathon this year after injuring your knee? You're a real glutton for punishment!"

2. Self-deprecating humor — People often say it about themselves with a laugh, acknowledging that they are choosing a very hard path.

"I signed up for another all-night study session. I guess I'm just a glutton for punishment."

3. Mild criticism — Sometimes it implies the person is making the same bad decisions repeatedly and not learning from them.

"She keeps getting back together with him even though he treats her badly. She's a glutton for punishment."

So the tone shifts slightly depending on context, but it is never deeply offensive. It's more wry and ironic than cruel.
Real-Life Examples to Make It Click

Here are situations where you would naturally use this idiom:

  • A person who works 80-hour weeks by choice, takes on extra projects, and never rests — even though no one is making them do it.
  • An athlete who trains through pain and injury and keeps pushing their body to its limits for the love of the sport.
  • A student who always picks the hardest courses, even when easier options are available.
  • Someone who keeps starting arguments or putting themselves in stressful situations unnecessarily.
  • A writer who keeps submitting their work to places that have rejected them dozens of times and just keeps going.

In all these cases, the person is choosing hardship. That choice is the heart of the idiom.

The most important thing that makes this idiom work is the element of voluntary choice.

A glutton for punishment is not someone who suffers because life forces them to. We wouldn't call someone whose house burned down "a glutton for punishment." That was not their choice.

It is about someone who could avoid the difficulty but doesn't — and seems almost to seek it out, again and again.

The word glutton comes from the Old French word glouton and the Latin gluto, both meaning someone who devours excessively. The concept of gluttony — consuming far more than you need — was historically considered one of the seven deadly sins in Christian tradition, tied to a lack of self-control.

Over time, English speakers began using "glutton" metaphorically to describe someone who takes in excess of anything, not just food. You can be a glutton for attention, for work, for praise, or for knowledge. ("She's a glutton for books" is perfectly understandable English.)

The specific phrase "glutton for punishment" grew naturally from this — someone who consumes far more suffering or hardship than any person reasonably should.

The idiom is a noun phrase, used like this:

  • "He is a glutton for punishment." ✅
  • "She must be a glutton for punishment to take that job." ✅
  • "Only a glutton for punishment would climb that mountain twice." ✅

It's always in the form: a glutton for punishment (with the article "a").

A glutton for punishment is someone who willingly and repeatedly takes on pain, difficulty, or hardship — far beyond what most people would tolerate — almost as though they enjoy it or simply can't help themselves.

Once you understand this idiom, you'll start noticing it everywhere — in sports commentary, in casual conversation, in books, and in films. It's one of those idioms that perfectly captures a very human type of person: the one who always takes the hardest road, even when an easier one is right there.
7029:
Gluttonous describes someone (or something) that consumes far more than what is needed or reasonable — driven by greed and a total lack of self-control. It is an intensely negative word. It does not just mean "eating a lot" or "wanting more." It means consuming in a way that is excessive, shameless, and greedy.

Think of it this way: if a normal person eats until they are full and stops, a gluttonous person keeps going — not because they are still hungry, but because they simply cannot (or will not) stop themselves.
The Two Ways It Is Used

1. Literally — About Food and Eating

This is the most common and traditional use. A gluttonous person eats enormous amounts of food, far beyond their body's need, and they do it selfishly and greedily.

"He was so gluttonous that he ate three full meals meant for the entire family by himself."

"Her gluttonous eating habits shocked everyone at the dinner table."

The key idea here is excess + greed + no self-restraint. It is not about being a big eater — it is about being an uncontrollably greedy eater.

2. Figuratively — About Anything Consumed Greedily

Gluttonous is also used beyond food. It can describe an obsessive, greedy craving for anything — power, money, attention, pleasure, or resources.

"The gluttonous corporation bought up every small business in town, never satisfied."

"He had a gluttonous appetite for fame — no amount of recognition was ever enough."

In this sense, you are calling someone insatiably greedy — not just about food, but about life in general.

Gluttonous is never a neutral word. It always carries strong disapproval and judgment. When you call someone gluttonous, you are saying they are:

  • Greedy — they want more than their fair share
  • Selfish — their consumption often comes at a cost to others
  • Without discipline — they have surrendered control to their desire
  • Shameless — they do not seem bothered by their excess

This is why gluttony has historically been considered a moral failing, not just a bad habit.
The Difference Between "Gluttonous" and Similar Words

• Hungry — you need food. Gluttonous — you consume far beyond need.
  • Greedy — greedy is broad (wanting more of anything). Gluttonous is more vivid and visceral — it paints a picture of unrestrained, animal-like consumption.
  • Voracious — this also means consuming a lot, but it is far less negative. You can call someone voraciously curious as a compliment. You would never call someone gluttonously curious — gluttonous is almost always an insult.
  • Indulgent — mild and sometimes positive (an indulgent dessert). Gluttonous is never mild or positive.

Knowing the related words helps cement the meaning:

  • Glutton (noun) — the person who is gluttonous. "He is a glutton."
  • Gluttony (noun) — the quality or act of being gluttonous. "Gluttony is considered one of the seven deadly sins."
  • Gluttonously (adverb) — in a gluttonous manner. "She ate gluttonously."
  • Gluttonous (adjective) — the describing word. "A gluttonous feast."
One Line to Remember It Forever

Gluttonous = excessively and greedily consuming, well beyond need, with no self-control.

If you ever see this word, picture someone who has everything they need but keeps grabbing for more anyway — not out of necessity, but out of pure, unchecked greed. That image is gluttonous.
